short_description: Romano-Byzantine basilica crowning the summit of Montmartre.

beats.script_body: On the night of August 24, 1944, as Allied forces approached Paris, the German military governor was ordered to destroy the city. General von Choltitz defied the order. From the steps of Sacré-Cœur, Parisians watched the tricolour raised again over a liberated city.

On the evening of August 24, 1944, as Allied troops neared the capital, the German commander received orders to raze Paris. General von Choltitz refused. From the heights of Montmartre, Parisians witnessed the tricolour unfurled once more above a city freed from occupation.

short_description: Temple of the Republic — where revolutionary ideals were forged into national identity.

beats.script_body: Voltaire's remains were brought here in a triumphal procession in 1791, as Parisians declared this church a secular temple to the great men of France. The debates over who deserved burial here shaped the ideals of the French Republic and earned it the title Temple of the Nation.

It was Voltaire whose remains were carried here in a grand procession in 1791, as the people of Paris transformed this church into a secular shrine to France's greatest citizens. The fierce debates over who merited interment here forged the ideals of the Republic and gave it the name Temple of the Nation.

Voltaire and Rousseau lie entombed here, face to face for eternity — two philosophers whose rival visions of liberty and society ignited the French Revolution. The Panthéon became the Republic's answer to royal burial at Saint-Denis, a monument to merit over bloodline.

short_description: Historic apartment on Place des Vosges where Victor Hugo lived for sixteen years.

beats.script_body: Victor Hugo lived in this apartment from 1832 to 1848. Located on the Place des Vosges, Paris's oldest planned square, it was from this writing desk that Hugo penned much of Les Misérables and shaped French literary history.

short_description: Victor Hugo's historic 17th-century residence on Place des Vosges.

beats.script_body: Hugo was more than a novelist — he was a politician, artist, and visionary. His speeches from exile on the Channel Islands rallied opposition to Napoleon III, and his funeral in 1885 drew two million mourners through the streets of Paris.

short_description: Paris's most beloved public garden, created in 1612 for Marie de Médicis.

beats.script_body: Created in 1612 for Marie de Médicis, the Jardin du Luxembourg is the most cherished park in Paris. It served as a royal garden, a Revolutionary tribunal ground, and even a Luftwaffe headquarters during the German occupation.

short_description: Historic public garden — entered from the northeast gate near the Panthéon.

beats.script_body: The Grand Bassin at the center of the Jardin du Luxembourg has been a beloved gathering spot for centuries. Children push toy sailboats across the octagonal pond with sticks, a tradition dating back over a hundred years.

short_description: Historic capital of Normandy, where Joan of Arc was tried and burned.

beats.script_body: Rouen's old market square marks the site where Joan of Arc was burned at the stake on May 30, 1431. The English occupiers condemned her as a heretic — but France later rehabilitated her, and she was canonized as a saint in 1920.

short_description: Brussels' central square, far outside Paris's geofence.

beats.script_body: The Grand-Place was nearly destroyed by French bombardment in 1695 under Louis XIV. The guilds rebuilt it in just four years, creating the ornate Baroque façades that earned it UNESCO World Heritage status in 1998.

short_description: Dramatic chalk cliffs on the Normandy coast, far outside Paris's geofence.

beats.script_body: The white chalk cliffs of Étretat have inspired artists since Monet painted them in the 1880s. The natural stone arch called the Porte d'Aval was described by Maupassant as an elephant dipping its trunk into the sea.

short_description: Final resting place of Molière, Chopin, and Jim Morrison.
Where the storming of the Bastille ignited the French Revolution.
164-foot triumphal arch honouring those who fought for France.

beats.script_body: Napoleon commissioned the Arc de Triomphe in 1806 but never saw it finished — it was completed in 1836, fifteen years after his death. Beneath its vault lies the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, whose eternal flame has burned without interruption since 1923.

short_description: France's national naval museum at the Palais de Chaillot.

beats.script_body: The Musée de la Marine houses scale models of every major French warship since Louis XIV. The museum's prized exhibit is the gilded royal barge built for Napoleon's wedding to Marie Louise in 1810.

short_description: Underground ossuary holding the remains of six million Parisians.

beats.script_body: When the Les Innocents cemetery collapsed into neighbouring basements in 1786, authorities transferred millions of bones into abandoned limestone quarries beneath the city. You can still see musket ball marks on skulls from the Revolution.

short_description: Grand palace housing the French Senate, built for Marie de Médicis.

beats.script_body: The Palais du Luxembourg was built in 1615 for Marie de Médicis in a style reminiscent of the Pitti Palace in Florence. During the Revolution it became a prison, and the Directoire governed France from its chambers before Napoleon seized power.

poi_name: Du Pain et des Idées «The Original»
short_description: Legendary Canal Saint-Martin bakery — home of the pain des amis.

beats.script_body:
Du Pain et des Idées has been baking in this 19th-century shop since Christophe Vasseur left his advertising career in 2002. The rivalry with neighbouring boulangeries along the canal is fierce — locals call it the "Guerre des Croissants." Pro tip: try the pain des amis. It's Vasseur's secret weapon.

As Christophe Vasseur once said: "We don't compete — we just bake with more soul."

poi_name: Le Jules Verne — Paris's Crème de la Crème
short_description: Fine dining with accented characters: café, naïve, résumé, jalapeño.

beats.script_body:
Le Jules Verne brought haute cuisine to the Eiffel Tower's second floor in 1983. Chef Frédéric Anton's philosophy: «la cuisine est un art» — cooking is an art. The restaurant's pièce de résistance was always the dégustation menu.

short_description: Island in the Seine, birthplace of Paris over two thousand years ago.

beats.script_body: The Île de la Cité was once a marshy island where the Parisii tribe built their settlement around 250 BC. Today it holds Notre-Dame, the Conciergerie, and Sainte-Chapelle — the spiritual and judicial heart of France for over a millennium.

The Conciergerie on the Île de la Cité served as the main prison during the Reign of Terror. Marie Antoinette spent her final days in a damp cell here before being carted to the guillotine on October 16, 1793.

During the great floods of 1910, the Seine rose over eight metres and submerged the streets around the Île de la Cité. Thousands of Parisians were displaced, and bodies from riverside cemeteries were washed into the current.

short_description: Art museum in the Tuileries housing Monet's Water Lilies.

beats.script_body: In 1922, Monet donated eight monumental Water Lilies panels to France on the condition they be displayed in curved rooms that immersed the viewer. The Orangerie was redesigned to his specifications — it remains one of the most intimate art experiences in the world.

Monet stipulated in his donation agreement that the Water Lilies must never be moved from the Orangerie's oval rooms. Every panel remains exactly where he intended, curved to envelop the viewer in an endless horizon of colour.

The Tuileries garden surrounding the Orangerie was designed by André Le Nôtre in 1664, the same landscape architect who created Versailles. The garden blooms year-round with seasonal displays that Le Nôtre personally planned.

The museum's lower gallery houses the Walter-Guillaume collection of Impressionist and Post-Impressionist masterworks. Paul Guillaume amassed the collection in the 1920s, hosting the most exclusive salons in Paris.

short_description: Iron lattice tower on the Champ de Mars.

beats.script_body: The Eiffel Tower was nearly demolished in 1909. It was saved because the military used it as a radio transmission tower — intercepting enemy messages during World War I.
A completely new hidden history take on the Eiffel Tower focusing on the secret apartment at the top that Gustave Eiffel built for himself.

short_description: The start of the 1.9-kilometre grand avenue from Place de la Concorde to the Arc de Triomphe.

beats.script_body: Hidden history beat for the Champs-Élysées. The tree-lined promenade was originally a swampy field until Marie de Médicis had it drained and planted with elms in 1616 as an extension of the Tuileries Garden.

Architecture beat for the Champs-Élysées. The avenue passes dozens of historically significant buildings, each with distinct architectural styles spanning four centuries of Parisian construction from the Grand Palais to the Arc de Triomphe.
Local legends beat for the Champs-Élysées. Legend has it a ghostly carriage of Marie Antoinette races down the avenue at midnight, still fleeing the mob that dragged her from Versailles.
Food beat for the Champs-Élysées. The avenue and its side streets are lined with bistros, pâtisseries, and cafés that have served Parisians since the Belle Époque.
Art beat for the Champs-Élysées. Street artists along the avenue create charcoal portraits of historical figures, blending ancien régime grandeur with contemporary Parisian expression.

Dark history beat for the Champs-Élysées. The Place de la Concorde at the avenue's eastern end was the site of the guillotine during the Terror — Paris executed Louis XVI, Marie Antoinette, and over a thousand others here.
Literary beat for the Champs-Élysées. Victor Hugo, Émile Zola, and Marcel Proust all strolled this avenue and wrote about the buildings along it in their most celebrated works.
Religious beat for the Champs-Élysées. Within walking distance lie three of the most historically important churches in Paris: La Madeleine, Saint-Germain-l'Auxerrois, and Saint-Roch.
Music beat for the Champs-Élysées. The Théâtre des Champs-Élysées on a nearby side street is where Stravinsky's Rite of Spring premiered in 1913, provoking a riot in the audience.
Revolutionary beat for the Champs-Élysées. Every landmark along this avenue played a role in the birth of the French Republic — from the first revolutionary marches to the Liberation parade of 1944.
Nature beat for the Champs-Élysées. The promenade begins and ends in green spaces — the Tuileries Garden and the wooded paths around the Arc de Triomphe — leafy bookends to a historic walk.
Shopping beat for the Champs-Élysées. The avenue has been a commercial hub since the 18th century and remains Paris's most famous shopping destination, from Louis Vuitton to Ladurée.

short_description: Beaux-Arts bridge connecting the Champs-Élysées quarter to Les Invalides.

beats.script_body: Short.

The Pont Alexandre III, spanning the Seine between the Grand Palais and Les Invalides, is widely regarded as the most ornate bridge in Paris. Named after Tsar Alexander III to celebrate the Franco-Russian Alliance, the foundation stone was laid by his son Nicholas II in 1896. The bridge was completed in time for the 1900 Exposition Universelle, during which engineers discovered that the original builders had used steel from the Schneider-Creusot foundry, the same works that produced French artillery. The bridge's distinctive Beaux-Arts style features gilded Fames sculptures on its four pylons, Art Nouveau lampposts, and cherubs representing the sciences, arts, commerce, and industry. During construction, workers found remnants of an 18th-century quay wall and medieval mooring rings from the river trade era. The bridge offers some of the best views of the Eiffel Tower and the dome of Les Invalides, making it a favourite spot for photographers and couples alike. The Franco-Russian Alliance it commemorates was a diplomatic masterstroke by Foreign Minister Delcassé, who saw Russia as a counterweight to Bismarck's Germany — a partnership sealed in champagne at the Kremlin. On summer evenings, you can see bateaux-mouches gliding beneath the arches while the banks of the Seine host picnickers and booksellers, and music drifts from the floating clubs moored downstream near the Bibliothèque nationale.

short_description: France's national library, one of the oldest in the world.

beats.script_body: The Bibliothèque nationale de France traces its origins to the royal library of Charles V in 1368. The Richelieu site's Salle Labrouste reading room, with its nine ceramic domes supported by slender iron columns, is one of the most magnificent rooms in Europe.

The library's Oval Room was modelled after the reading room of the British Museum. Henri Labrouste spent twenty years perfecting the ironwork — it became his life's obsession and a masterpiece of 19th-century structural innovation.

short_description: Neoclassical temple-church modelled after the Maison Carrée at Nîmes.

beats.script_body: La Madeleine was commissioned by Napoleon in 1806 as a temple to the glory of his Grande Armée. The neoclassical design, with 52 Corinthian columns each 20 metres tall, was modelled after Roman temples. The church sits on a raised platform above the Place de la Madeleine, requiring worshippers to climb a monumental staircase.

Napoleon's original vision for La Madeleine was a secular temple of military glory, not a church. The building changed purpose multiple times — a stock exchange, a railway station, a national library were all proposed — before finally being consecrated as a Catholic church in 1842. Cavaille-Coll's grand organ inside is considered one of the finest in Paris, and Chopin's funeral was held here in 1849.

short_description: Major aquarium beneath the Trocadéro gardens facing the Eiffel Tower.

beats.script_body: The shark tunnel at the centre of the aquarium holds 700,000 litres of seawater and is home to over 500 species of marine life including nurse sharks, rays, and jellyfish. Opened in 1867 as the world's first public aquarium, it was the most ambitious exhibit of its kind.

The aquarium sits beneath the Trocadéro, on the site of old quarries that once supplied limestone for Haussmann's grand boulevards. Stone from these tunnels was used to build the very buildings that transformed Paris in the 19th century.

short_description: Paris's legendary football stadium, home of Paris Saint-Germain since 1974.

beats.script_body: The Parc des Princes opened in its current form in 1972, designed by architect Roger Taillibert with a dramatic cantilevered roof that needs no internal pillars. The site has hosted football since 1897 — when the original velodrome was built — and PSG's move here in 1974 transformed a cycling venue into one of European football's most intimidating grounds.
